From Static Context to Calibrated Interactive RL: Mitigating Distribution Shift in Multi-turn Dialogue with Aligned Simulator

Xiaohua Wang  Jiakang Yuan11footnotemark: 1  Zisu Huang  Muzhao Tian  Changze Lv Kaitao Song  Chen Tao  Xiaoqing Zheng Fudan University   xhwang24@m.fudan.edu.cn ††thanks: These authors contributed equally.††thanks: Corresponding author.
Abstract

A long-standing goal of the research community is to develop highly interactive LLM-based dialogue agents. Recent research focuses on optimizing policies based on fixed offline logs (Static Context RL) or using a prompt-based simulator (Interactive RL). In this work, we theoretically show that both paradigms are fundamentally limited by context distribution shift—a mismatch between dialogue histories observed during training and those encountered in real conversations. This shift compounds quadratically over turns and severely degrades dialogue quality. Specifically, we attribute this shift to two distinct sources: (i) policy-induced shift, arising from training on static histories rather than self-generated trajectories; and (ii) simulator-induced shift, stemming from discrepancies between simulated and real human behaviors. To address these challenges, we propose Calibrated Interactive RL, a unified framework that couples interactive RL with simulator alignment. By aligning the simulator with human interaction patterns, our approach reduces the sim-to-real gap and mitigates compounding distribution shifts. Experiments across multiple dialogue tasks confirm our theoretical analysis: (i) Interactive RL significantly outperforms the Static Context baseline by mitigating policy distribution shift; and (ii) calibrating simulators with our alignment method further bridges the sim-to-real gap, yielding state-of-the-art downstream performance.

1 Introduction

A long-standing goal in the research community is to develop highly interactive LLM-based dialogue agents that can sustain coherent, safe, and goal-directed multi-turn conversations Li et al. (2025); Laban et al. (2025). To advance this objective, recent work has increasingly adopted reinforcement learning (RL) to align the model’s behavior with human preferences Ouyang et al. (2022); Bai et al. (2022a); Bai et al. (2022b). Broadly, existing approaches can be categorized into two primary paradigms: Static Context RL Lee et al. (2023); Hong et al. (2023); Verma et al. (2022); Snell et al. (2022); Rafailov et al. (2023) and Interactive RL Wu et al. (2025); Shani et al. (2024); Carta et al. (2023). The former optimizes policy models using fixed offline contexts (i.e., serialized conversation histories), without the need to generate the preceding turns. In contrast, the latter addresses the inherently dynamic nature of dialogue by employing a prompt-based user simulator, thereby enabling agents to engage in multi-turn interactions within a closed-loop learning framework.

Despite their preliminary efficacy, these approaches face fundamental limitations as shown in Table 1. On one hand, static context methods disrupt the essential RL interaction loop, thereby undermining the interactive capabilities of dialogue agents. On the other hand, while interactive approaches attempt to bridge this gap, they typically rely on prompt-based simulators that fail to capture the stochasticity, ambiguity, and noise inherent in real user inputs. This deficiency creates a significant sim-to-real gap, ultimately compromising the policy’s applicability in real-world scenarios.

In this work, we establish the theoretical foundations for addressing these challenges. We formally demonstrate that existing paradigms are fundamentally constrained by context distribution shift—a discrepancy between dialogue histories observed during training and those encountered in real conversations. We show that this shift compounds quadratically over turns, severely degrading dialogue quality. Specifically, we decompose this phenomenon into two distinct sources: (i) Policy-induced shift is caused by the mismatch between fixed offline histories and self-generated trajectories; and (ii) Simulator-induced shift arises from the structural divergence between prompt-based simulators and real human behaviors.

To this end, we introduce Calibrated Interactive RL, a unified framework that couples interactive RL with the aligned simulator. Specifically, we first align the user simulator using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on real human multi-turn interactions, enabling it to capture realistic human behaviors such as clarification-seeking, stubbornness, and strict goal-adherence. Building upon this calibrated simulator, we leverage interactive RL to optimize the policy on self-generated trajectories, thereby explicitly addressing the policy-induced distribution shift and allowing the agent to learn essential error-recovery skills.

Empirically, our analysis reveals that standard prompt-based simulators exhibit severe behavioral artifacts, most notably sycophancy—a tendency to blindly accept incorrect agent outputs or prematurely leak ground-truth information. This effectively trivializes the RL interaction loop and inevitably leads to reward hacking, where the policy learns to exploit the simulator’s permissiveness rather than solving the actual task. By treating the simulator as a trainable agent and performing behavioral cloning on high-quality offline logs, our Simulator Alignment framework rigorously grounds the simulation in human reality. Our experiments demonstrate that Interactive RL consistently outperforms the Static Context baseline and that training with our Aligned Simulators yields further significant gains. These results highlight the need for both closing the interaction loop and explicitly grounding simulations.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We establish the theoretical foundation for multi-turn dialogue RL, reveal the source of the context distribution shift in existing RL methods, and mathematically demonstrate that these shifts compound quadratically over turns.

  • •

    We propose Calibrated Interactive RL, a unified framework that couples interactive policy optimization with simulator alignment. We introduce an SFT-based calibration method that grounds the user simulator in real human behavioral distributions, eliminating simulation artifacts (e.g., sycophancy) and effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap.

  • •

    Extensive experiments demonstrate that Interactive RL consistently outperforms Static Context baselines. Furthermore, explicitly calibrating the simulator yields significant additional gains, highlighting the critical importance of preventing reward hacking by grounding simulations in human reality.

2 Related Work

2.1 Reinforcement Learning for Multi-turn Dialogue

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has established itself as the cornerstone for aligning LLMs with human intent Ouyang et al. (2022); Bai et al. (2022a). In the context of dialogue systems, existing approaches can be broadly categorized into Static Context RL and Interactive RL. Static Context RL optimizes policies based on static, offline conversation logs Shi et al. (2024); Hong et al. (2023); Snell et al. (2022). For instance, Charlie et al. (Snell et al., 2022) applies implicit Q-learning to fixed language datasets. Although effective for single-turn instruction following, these static context approaches suffer from distribution shift and the inability to correct generation errors that compound over turns—a known limitation in sequential decision-making Levine et al. (2020). In contrast, Interactive RL mainly utilizes a simulator to close the interaction loop and allows the agent to learn from its own generation trajectory Shani et al. (2024); Zhou et al. (2024). For example, CollabLLM Wu et al. (2025) utilizes a prompt-based user simulator to train agents on online collaborative traces. Distinct from existing approaches, we theoretically prove that existing methods suffer from context distribution shift between training and those encountered in real conversations. Besides, Calibrated Interactive RL is introduced to bridge the sim-to-real gap by aligning the user simulator via discriminator-derived realism rewards.

2.2 Distribution Shift and Exposure Bias

The discrepancy between training on ground-truth history (i.e., teacher forcing) and generating on the model’s own history (i.e., student forcing) is a fundamental challenge in sequence generation, known as exposure bias Bengio et al. (2015); Ranzato et al. (2015). In the context of decision-making, this phenomenon parallels the distribution shift analyzed in imitation learning. Ross et al. Ross et al. (2011) demonstrated that behavior cloning (i.e., offline training) results in errors that accumulate quadratically (O⁡(H2)O(H^{2})) with the horizon HH, whereas interactive expert guidance (i.e., Dagger) can reduce this to linear growth. While recent works have analyzed this shift in the context of single-turn reasoning chains Wang et al. (2023), our work formally extends this analysis to the multi-turn dialogue setting. We derive a rigorous bound illustrating how static context training fails to generalize to the dynamic distribution induced by the policy’s own actions during prolonged interactions.

2.3 LLM-based User Simulators

Employing LLM-based simulators as surrogates for human users has emerged as a prominent trend for scalable evaluation and training Shi et al. (2019); Tseng et al. (2021); Hu et al. (2023); Gandhi et al. (2026). Park et al. Park et al. (2023) demonstrated that LLM agents can simulate believable social behaviors, and automated evaluation frameworks like MT-Bench Bai et al. (2024) and AlpacaEval Dubois et al. (2023) utilize LLM judges to proxy human preferences. In the domain of interactive training, recent studies have employed "Self-Play" or simulator-based RL to improve task performance Shao et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2024); Silver et al. (2017). However, uncalibrated simulators often exhibit distinct artifacts, such as "sycophancy" (agreeing with the model’s errors) Sharma et al. (2023) or unrealistic persona consistency Shanahan et al. (2023). These artifacts can be exploited by the policy agent during RL training, leading to reward hacking Wang and others (2025) where the agent optimizes for simulator approval rather than genuine task success. Unlike previous works that use off-the-shelf LLMs as simulators, we propose a Simulator Alignment framework, treating the simulator as a trainable agent optimized to minimize the sim-to-real gap, thereby ensuring that interactive training yields robust real-world performance.

3 Distribution Shift in Multi-turn RL

In this section, we formally analyze the distribution shifts inherent in multi-turn dialogue training. We derive two fundamental bounds that motivate our proposed Calibrated Interactive RL framework. First, we show that standard offline training (i.e., Static Context RL) induces a biased objective due to compounding policy deviations. Second, we demonstrate that while Interactive RL addresses this by closing the interaction loop, it relies on simulator fidelity, as simulator errors also accumulate quadratically. These insights underscore the necessity of our Simulator Alignment approach. Detailed proofs are provided in Appendix A.

3.1 Setup and Notation

We consider an episodic dialogue environment with a finite horizon HH. Let st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} denote the environment state and at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} the dialogue agent’s action at time tt. A history ht=(s0,a0,…,st)h_{t}=(s_{0},a_{0},\dots,s_{t}) represents the trajectory up to time tt. Policies map histories to distributions over actions; we denote the behavior policy that generated the offline logs as πdata\pi_{\text{data}}, and the learned policy as π\pi.

Let dtπ​(h)d^{\pi}_{t}(h) be the marginal distribution over histories at time tt induced by policy π\pi. To analyze the simulation gap, we distinguish between the transition dynamics of the real user, denoted by the operator 𝒯real\mathcal{T}_{\text{real}}, and the user simulator, 𝒯sim\mathcal{T}_{\text{sim}}. We assume rewards are bounded such that |r⁡(s,a)|≤Rmax|r(s,a)|\leq R_{\max}. The objective is to maximize the finite-horizon return J⁡(π)=𝔼τ∼pπ​[∑t=0H−1rt]J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\pi}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}r_{t}\right].

Based on the notation, Static Context RL decouples policy optimization from state generation. Its updates and gradient estimators are computed using contexts h∼dtdatah\sim d^{\text{data}}_{t} sampled from the offline distribution dtdatad^{\text{data}}_{t}, rather than the on-policy distribution dtπd^{\pi}_{t}. Consequently, the optimization is fundamentally off-policy with respect to the state distribution, as it ignores how π\pi influences future histories. On the contrary, Interactive RL maintains the closed interaction loop. The objective is evaluated under the distribution h∼dtπh\sim d^{\pi}_{t} induced by the policy’s interaction with the environment, thereby capturing the consequences of its own actions.

3.2 Error Source I: Compounding Policy Shift in Static Context RL

We first quantify the performance degradation caused by training on static contexts. Let π′\pi^{\prime} denote a reference policy (e.g., the data-generating policy πdata\pi_{\text{data}}) and π\pi denote the learned policy. We define two divergence terms: the history distribution mismatch Δt=‖dtπ−dtπ′‖1\Delta_{t}=\|d^{\pi}_{t}-d^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}\|_{1}, and the per-step policy deviation εt=𝔼h∼dtπ′∥π(⋅∣h)−π′(⋅∣h)∥1\varepsilon_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{h\sim d^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}}\|\pi(\cdot\mid h)-\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid h)\|_{1}.

Theorem 3.1 (Performance Difference via Policy Shift).

For any two policies π,π′\pi,\pi^{\prime} and finite horizon HH, the difference in expected return is bounded by:

|J⁡(π)−J⁡(π′)|≤Rmax​∑t=0H−1(Δt+εt).\small|J(\pi)-J(\pi^{\prime})|\leq R_{\max}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}(\Delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}). (1)

Furthermore, since Δt≤∑i=0t−1εi\Delta_{t}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}\varepsilon_{i}, the total error satisfies:

|J⁡(π)−J⁡(π′)|≤Rmax​∑i=0H−1(H−i)​εi.\small|J(\pi)-J(\pi^{\prime})|\leq R_{\max}\sum_{i=0}^{H-1}(H-i)\varepsilon_{i}. (2)

Proof Sketch. We decompose the return difference into a sum over time of divergences in the joint (history, action) distributions. As the environment transition operator is non-expansive in the ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm, distribution errors propagate linearly, yielding Δt+1≤Δt+εt\Delta_{t+1}\leq\Delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}. Summing this recurrence yields the quadratic bound. Detailed proofs are provided in Appendix A.

Theoretical Implication. Theorem 3.1 establishes that errors in Static Context RL compound quadratically (O⁡(H2)O(H^{2})). Small deviations εt\varepsilon_{t} in the policy at early turns accumulate into a large distribution shift Δt\Delta_{t}, pushing the agent into out-of-distribution states where it has never been trained. Static Context RL ignores Δt\Delta_{t}, optimizing only for local accuracy, and thus fails to guarantee long-horizon interactive performance.

Intuitive Explanation & Running Example. To intuitively understand this quadratic compounding effect, consider a conversational math tutoring scenario. Suppose the agent makes a minor logical error at turn t=1t=1 (a small policy deviation ε1\varepsilon_{1}). In a real interaction, the subsequent dialogue history will fundamentally diverge from the ground-truth offline logs (creating a large history mismatch Δ2\Delta_{2}), because the human user will likely point out the mistake or express confusion. However, a model trained purely via Static Context RL has only seen perfect, expert-guided trajectory histories. When thrust into this self-generated, flawed context during deployment, the agent lacks the essential error-recovery skills. Instead of correcting itself, it is prone to hallucinate further (yielding large ε2,ε3,…\varepsilon_{2},\varepsilon_{3},\dots). Consequently, an initially negligible mistake cascades dynamically over the horizon HH, leading to catastrophic failure. Interactive RL mitigates this by explicitly exposing the agent to its own mistakes during training, thereby teaching it how to navigate back to the correct path.

3.3 Error Source II: Simulator-Real Distribution Shift

While Interactive RL resolves the policy distribution shift by training on dtπd^{\pi}_{t}, it introduces a new source of error: the discrepancy between the simulator 𝒯sim\mathcal{T}_{\text{sim}} and the real user 𝒯real\mathcal{T}_{\text{real}}. To isolate the impact of simulator fidelity, we analyze the gap for a fixed policy π\pi. We define the simulator error at time tt as the expected divergence in transition dynamics under the real joint distribution: δt=𝔼(h,a)∼qtreal∥𝒯real(⋅|h,a)−𝒯sim(⋅|h,a)∥1\delta_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{(h,a)\sim q^{\text{real}}_{t}}\|\mathcal{T}_{\text{real}}(\cdot|h,a)-\mathcal{T}_{\text{sim}}(\cdot|h,a)\|_{1}, where qtreal​(h,a)=dreal,tπ​(h)​π​(a|h)q^{\text{real}}_{t}(h,a)=d^{\pi}_{\text{real},t}(h)\pi(a|h).

Theorem 3.2 (Sim-to-Real Gap).

For any policy π\pi and horizon HH, the performance gap caused by the simulator is bounded by:

|Jreal​(π)−Jsim​(π)|≤Rmax​∑i=0H−1(H−i)​δi.\small|J_{\text{real}}(\pi)-J_{\text{sim}}(\pi)|\leq R_{\max}\sum_{i=0}^{H-1}(H-i)\delta_{i}. (3)

Proof Sketch We upper-bound the performance gap between the real and simulated environments by aggregating the marginal distribution shifts over the horizon. Leveraging the non-expansive nature of stochastic transition operators under the ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm, we show that the distribution divergence at any step is bounded by the sum of the propagated error from the previous step and the immediate local simulation error. This leads to the recurrence Δt+1env≤Δtenv+δt\Delta_{t+1}^{\text{env}}\leq\Delta_{t}^{\text{env}}+\delta_{t}, which telescopes to yield the final cumulative bound. The complete derivation is detailed in Appendix A.

Theoretical Implication. This result highlights that simulator misalignment is as detrimental as policy misalignment. Even if interactive training is used, a simulator that deviates from human behavior (i.e., δt>0\delta_{t}>0) causes the training objective to diverge from the real-world objective at a rate of O⁡(H2​δ)O(H^{2}\delta). This formally justifies our Simulator Alignment approach: minimizing δt\delta_{t} is a theoretical prerequisite for robust interactive learning.

Intuitive Explanation & Running Example. To see why standard interactive training is insufficient without simulator calibration, consider the well-documented behavioral artifacts of uncalibrated LLM simulators, such as “sycophancy” (blind agreement) Sharma et al. (2023). Suppose the dialogue agent proposes a highly flawed document edit. A real human user would reject the edit and demand a revision (representing a specific transition in 𝒯real\mathcal{T}_{\text{real}}). In contrast, a naive, uncalibrated simulator might enthusiastically accept the flawed edit, complimenting the agent (a severely divergent transition in 𝒯sim\mathcal{T}_{\text{sim}}, yielding a large local error δt\delta_{t}). By interacting with this flawed simulator over multiple turns, the agent receives false-positive feedback and learns a degenerate policy that exploits the simulator’s permissiveness rather than actually solving the task—a phenomenon closely related to reward hacking Wang and others (2025). As shown by our bound, this simulator-induced delusion accumulates quadratically over the conversation length HH. Therefore, aligning the simulator to accurately reflect human stubbornness, constraints, and feedback patterns is not merely an engineering trick, but a fundamental mathematical requirement to ensure that the surrogate objective Jsim​(π)J_{\text{sim}}(\pi) faithfully proxies the true real-world objective Jreal​(π)J_{\text{real}}(\pi).

4 Calibrated Interactive RL

Motivated by the compounding distribution shifts identified in Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, it is evident that a robust multi-turn dialogue agent must simultaneously address both policy-induced and simulator-induced errors. To this end, we propose Calibrated Interactive RL. As shown in Figure 1 (b), our method operates in two distinct phases: (1) Simulator Calibration, where we train a goal-guided user simulator via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to mimic human interaction patterns; and (2) Interactive Policy Optimization, where the dialogue agent is trained within this calibrated environment using memory-efficient RL to maximize task success.

4.1 Phase I: Simulator Calibration via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)

The primary bottleneck in standard interactive RL is the simulator-induced shift (δt\delta_{t}). Conventional prompt-based simulators frequently fail to exhibit the specific intent, cognitive blind spots, or "stubbornness" of real users. To minimize this sim-to-real gap, we formulate the simulator as a trainable agent and explicitly align it with human behavioral distributions using historical multi-turn data.

Goal-Guided Simulation Context. Unlike the dialogue policy, which must infer the user’s intent dynamically, the user simulator functions as an environmental "Teacher" and thus requires access to the full ground truth. Let 𝒟={(x,y∗,hreal)}\mathcal{D}=\{(x,y^{*},h_{\text{real}})\} denote a dataset containing the initial instruction xx, the ground-truth solution y∗y^{*}, and the reference human history hrealh_{\text{real}}. We condition the simulator πϕsim\pi_{\phi}^{\text{sim}} on an oracle context Itsim=[x,y∗,ht,at]I_{t}^{\text{sim}}=[x,y^{*},h_{t},a_{t}]. This privileged information allows the simulator to consistently verify whether the agent’s current action ata_{t} aligns with the target y∗y^{*} and to provide feedback or corrections consistent with the reference intent, without hallucinating diverging goals.

Calibration via Behavioral Cloning. To ensure the simulator accurately reflects human transition dynamics 𝒯real\mathcal{T}_{\text{real}}, we optimize the simulator parameters ϕ\phi using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on the real user turns from 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Specifically, we minimize the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the reference human responses utu_{t} given the oracle context and the dialogue history up to turn tt:

ℒCalibration​(ϕ)=−𝔼(x,y∗,hreal,areal)∼𝒟​[∑tlog⁡πϕsim​(ut∣x,y∗,ht,at)]\small\mathcal{L}_{\text{Calibration}}(\phi)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^{*},h_{\text{real}},a_{\text{real}})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\sum_{t}\log\pi_{\phi}^{\text{sim}}(u_{t}\mid x,y^{*},h_{t},a_{t})\right] (4)

By conditioning on both the ground-truth and the agent’s actual output the simulator learns to provide grounded feedback, such as asking for clarification, expressing partial understanding, or persistently rejecting incorrect solutions.

Mitigating Simulator Artifacts and Reward Hacking. The motivation for SFT calibration extends beyond mere behavioral realism; it also provides a critical defense against reward hackingWang and others (2025). Uncalibrated simulators frequently exhibit "sycophancy" (blindly agreeing with flawed logicSharma et al. (2023)), which RL agents rapidly exploit by generating confident but incorrect responses to trick the simulator into emitting unearned success signals. By rigorously grounding the simulator in actual human data, we eliminate these exploitable artifacts, ensuring the policy must make genuine progress to achieve high rewards.

4.2 Phase II: Interactive Policy Optimization

With the calibrated simulator πϕ∗sim\pi^{\text{sim}}_{\phi^{*}} frozen, we proceed to optimize the dialogue policy πθ\pi_{\theta}. This phase closes the interaction loop to address the policy-induced shift (Δt\Delta_{t}).

On-Policy Trajectory Generation. In contrast to Static Context RL, our agent generates full multi-turn trajectories by interacting dynamically with the aligned simulator. For an episode of length HH, the joint trajectory τ=(s0,a0,u0,…,aH−1,uH−1)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},u_{0},\dots,a_{H-1},u_{H-1}) is generated via alternating execution, as summarized in Algorithm 1. This ensures that the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} is trained on the exact state distribution dtπθd^{\pi_{\theta}}_{t} it dynamically visits, allowing it to naturally develop robust error-recovery and long-horizon planning strategies that are fundamentally unlearnable from static, off-policy logs.

Sparse Task Rewards. The quality of the interaction is measured solely by outcome success. We utilize a sparse reward signal RtaskR_{\text{task}} administered only at the final turn HH. Let y^\hat{y} be the final output produced by the agent (e.g., the refined document or final code):

R⁡(τ)={Score​(y^,y∗)at ​t=H0at ​t<H\small R(\tau)=\begin{cases}\text{Score}(\hat{y},y^{*})&\text{at }t=H\\ 0&\text{at }t<H\end{cases} (5)

For document editing tasks, Score​(⋅)\text{Score}(\cdot) is the BLEU metric; for math and coding tasks, it is a binary correctness indicator. This outcome-based supervision forces the agent to engage in meaningful information seeking. The policy πθ\pi_{\theta} is then optimized using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) Shao et al. (2024) to maximize the expected return 𝔼τ​[R​(τ)]\mathbb{E}_{\tau}[R(\tau)].

5 Experiments

We conduct extensive experiments to validate two core hypotheses: (1) Interactive RL significantly outperforms Static Context RL by mitigating the distribution shift between offline training contexts and on-policy generation; and (2) Simulator Alignment is critical for interactive training—optimizing the simulator to mimic human intent and natural interaction patterns leads to superior downstream policy performance.

5.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Benchmarks.

To rigorously evaluate the dynamic interaction capabilities of our framework, we employ two challenging multi-turn dialogue benchmarks inspired by recent collaborative agent evaluations Wu et al. (2025). These datasets are explicitly designed to test long-horizon planning, ambiguity resolution, and error recovery:

  • •

    MediumDocEdit-Chat (Collaborative Editing): Derived from document editing corpora, this task requires the agent to help a user iteratively refine a document. Unlike single-turn instruction following, user intents in this dataset are frequently ambiguous or incomplete. The agent must proactively ask clarifying questions, propose partial edits, and adapt to shifting user feedback over multiple turns. The primary objective evaluation metric is BLEU, calculated between the final model-refined document and the ground-truth target text.

  • •

    MATH-Chat (Conversational Reasoning): Adapted from the MATH dataset, this benchmark evaluates the agent’s ability to act as an interactive tutor. Instead of directly outputting the final answer, the agent must guide a simulated student (who may make logical errors or express confusion) step-by-step toward the correct solution. This requires robust reasoning scaffolding and the ability to correct trajectory deviations dynamically. The task success is measured by the final answer Accuracy (Acc.).

Models and Baselines.

To ensure a fair and controlled comparison, we utilize Gemma-3-4B-IT Gemma Team et al. (2024) as the foundational backbone for both the policy agent and the user simulator across all experiments. We systematically compare our full Calibrated Interactive RL framework against established paradigms and internal ablations, seamlessly mirroring the theoretical sources of distribution shift (as summarized in Table 2):

  • •

    Gemma-3-4B-IT (Base Model): The original instruction-tuned model without any multi-turn RL fine-tuning, acting as our zero-shot baseline.

  • •

    CollabLLM (Static RL): The state-of-the-art offline multi-turn RL method Wu et al. (2025). We faithfully reproduce this baseline using the official codebase, optimizing the Gemma-3 policy on static conversational logs using Multi-turn-aware Rewards. This represents the upper bound of the Static Context RL paradigm.

  • •

    Static Context: An ablation of our method where the policy is trained exclusively on fixed offline history distributions (h∼ddatah\sim d^{\text{data}}) without dynamic simulator rollouts.

  • •

    Ours (Naive Interactive): An ablation utilizing the full Interactive RL loop, but employing a basic, uncalibrated user simulator (prompting the Base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Qwen Team (2024) model without Phase I SFT). This isolates the impact of closing the interaction loop from the simulator’s behavioral fidelity.

  • •

    Ours (Calibrated Interactive): Our complete proposed framework, featuring on-policy trajectory generation against the Phase I SFT-aligned user simulator.

  • •

    Oracle (Proxy Human): An evaluation upper-bound representing the performance of the base policy when interacting with a privileged proxy human simulator that has direct access to the ground-truth targets.

Implementation Details.

In Phase I, the user simulator (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) is trained via SFT on 1,860 (MATH) and 16,028 (MediumDocEdit) multi-turn trajectories collected from an oracle Qwen3-235B Yang et al. (2025) simulator. In Phase II, the policy (Gemma-3-4B-IT) is optimized via GRPO on 32 GPUs with a group size of G=32G=32 samples per prompt and a global batch size of 8,192. We use a constant learning rate of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6} with Adam (β1=0.9,β2=0.98\beta_{1}{=}0.9,\beta_{2}{=}0.98) and asymmetric PPO-style clipping Schulman et al. (2017) (ϵ∈[0.2,0.28]\epsilon\in[0.2,0.28]). Full hyperparameter tables are provided in Appendix D.

Evaluation Metrics.

Following the evaluation protocol of CollabLLM, we assess performance along two primary dimensions. (1) Task Performance: Measured by BLEU for editing and Accuracy for math reasoning. (2) Efficiency: We report the average generation length (#Toks, in thousands of tokens), where lower values indicate more concise, natural conversational turns rather than monolithic document dumps. We additionally report the Average Score (arithmetic mean of BLEU and ACC) as a unified metric across domains. All experiments are repeated 3 times with different random seeds; we report mean ±\pm standard deviation.

5.2 Experimental Results

Table 2 summarizes the comprehensive results across both domains. Our proposed framework achieves the highest MATH-Chat accuracy (91.5%), substantially outperforming all baselines and even surpassing the Oracle reference (89.7%). In the following, we provide a detailed analysis of these empirical findings.

Interactive RL Beats Static Context RL.

Closing the interaction loop significantly improves task success: MATH-Chat accuracy rises from 85.0% (Static Context) to 89.3% (Naive Interactive), a gain of +4.3 points. This validates our theoretical analysis (Section 3): optimizing the policy on dynamically induced state distributions (h∼dπh\sim d^{\pi}) rather than fixed offline logs equips the agent with robust error-recovery skills and mitigates compounding distribution shifts. Qualitatively, interactive agents successfully rectify logical missteps dynamically, whereas static agents often hallucinate when user feedback deviates from their offline training distribution. To provide deeper intuition into the behavioral improvements, Figure 2 illustrates a qualitative analysis of successfully resolved cases on MATH-Chat. Our Calibrated Interactive RL agent effectively avoids degenerate "try-and-fail" loops, arriving at correct solutions in significantly fewer dialogue turns. We refer readers to Appendix F for comprehensive step-by-step case studies demonstrating the model’s enhanced structural understanding and proactive error-recovery strategies.

Calibrated Simulators are Essential for Interaction.

Merely closing the interaction loop is insufficient; aligning the simulator with human behavior yields further substantial gains. On MATH-Chat, calibrated training achieves 91.5% accuracy—a +2.2 improvement over the Naive Interactive baseline (89.3%) and notably surpassing even the Oracle (89.7%). This suggests our aligned simulator provides a highly effective and complementary training signal: by calibrating the simulator to maintain realistic persistence and avoid sycophantic behavior, the policy learns more robust reasoning strategies that generalize even beyond what a single proxy human would elicit.

Comparison with CollabLLM.

The state-of-the-art static baseline (CollabLLM, offline DPO) performs comparably to the vanilla base model on MATH-Chat (82.3% vs. 82.3%). This highlights a fundamental limitation of offline RL in multi-turn settings: without on-policy experience, the agent never observes how its responses shape subsequent dialogue turns. The superiority of all our interactive methods confirms that on-policy experience generation is a critical prerequisite for robust multi-turn optimization.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we established the theoretical foundations for the limitations of Static Context RL, formally proving that training on fixed offline logs induces a context distribution shift where errors compound quadratically over turns. To address this fundamental bottleneck, we proposed Calibrated Interactive RL, a unified framework that couples interactive training with rigorous simulator alignment. We demonstrated that simply closing the interaction loop is insufficient; the success of interactive learning critically depends on minimizing the sim-to-real gap. By treating the user simulator as a trainable agent and optimizing it to maximize a discriminator-derived realism reward, we effectively aligned the simulation environment with human interaction patterns. Our extensive experiments confirm that our framework not only mitigates policy-induced distribution shifts but also fosters robust information-seeking behaviors, significantly outperforming baselines relying on static contexts or uncalibrated simulators. This work highlights the necessity of high-fidelity, aligned simulation as a prerequisite for the next generation of interactive dialogue agents.

Appendix A Theoretical Proofs and Derivations

In this appendix, we provide full proofs for the theoretical claims presented in Section 3. We first restate the necessary notation and assumptions, then establish auxiliary lemmas regarding distributional divergence, and finally derive the bounds for Policy Mismatch (Theorem 3.1) and the Sim-to-Real Gap (Theorem 3.2).

A.1 Notation and Preliminaries

We consider a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined over histories to account for the non-Markovian nature of dialogue when viewed from the perspective of state-only transitions.

  • •

    Horizon: H∈ℕH\in\mathbb{N}. Time steps are indexed by t=0,…,H−1t=0,\dots,H-1.

  • •

    History: Let ht=(s0,a0,…,st)∈ℋh_{t}=(s_{0},a_{0},\dots,s_{t})\in\mathcal{H} denote the interaction history up to time tt.

  • •

    Distributions: Let dtπ​(h)d^{\pi}_{t}(h) denote the marginal distribution over histories at time tt induced by policy π\pi and the environment dynamics.

  • •

    Norms: Unless otherwise specified, ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} denotes the ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm (total variation distance) for probability distributions. For a function ff, ‖f‖∞=supx|f⁡(x)|\|f\|_{\infty}=\sup_{x}|f(x)|.

  • •

    Rewards: We assume a bounded reward function r⁡(h,a)r(h,a) such that |r⁡(h,a)|≤Rmax|r(h,a)|\leq R_{\max} for all h,ah,a.

A.2 Auxiliary Lemmas

We begin by establishing a decomposition lemma that bounds the divergence of a joint distribution in terms of the marginal distribution divergence and the conditional distribution divergence.

Lemma A.1 (Joint Distribution Decomposition).

Consider two joint distributions p⁡(x,y)=p⁡(x)​p​(y|x)p(x,y)=p(x)p(y|x) and q⁡(x,y)=q⁡(x)​q​(y|x)q(x,y)=q(x)q(y|x) over discrete domains 𝒳,𝒴\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}. Then:

‖p−q‖1≤‖p⁡(x)−q⁡(x)‖1+𝔼x∼q⁡(x)​[‖p⁡(y|x)−q⁡(y|x)‖1].\|p-q\|_{1}\leq\|p(x)-q(x)\|_{1}+\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q(x)}[\|p(y|x)-q(y|x)\|_{1}]. (6)
Proof.

By definition of the ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm:

‖p−q‖1\displaystyle\|p-q\|_{1} =∑x,y|p⁡(x)​p​(y|x)−q⁡(x)​q​(y|x)|\displaystyle=\sum_{x,y}|p(x)p(y|x)-q(x)q(y|x)|
=∑x,y|p⁡(x)​p​(y|x)−q⁡(x)​p​(y|x)+q⁡(x)​p​(y|x)−q⁡(x)​q​(y|x)|\displaystyle=\sum_{x,y}|p(x)p(y|x)-q(x)p(y|x)+q(x)p(y|x)-q(x)q(y|x)|
≤∑x,y|p⁡(x)−q⁡(x)​|p⁡(y|x)+∑x,yq⁡(x)|​p​(y|x)−q⁡(y|x)|\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x,y}|p(x)-q(x)|p(y|x)+\sum_{x,y}q(x)|p(y|x)-q(y|x)|
=∑x|p⁡(x)−q⁡(x)|​∑yp⁡(y|x)⏟=1+∑xq⁡(x)​∑y|p⁡(y|x)−q⁡(y|x)|\displaystyle=\sum_{x}|p(x)-q(x)|\underbrace{\sum_{y}p(y|x)}_{=1}+\sum_{x}q(x)\sum_{y}|p(y|x)-q(y|x)|
=‖p⁡(x)−q⁡(x)‖1+𝔼x∼q⁡(x)​[‖p⁡(y|x)−q⁡(y|x)‖1].\displaystyle=\|p(x)-q(x)\|_{1}+\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q(x)}[\|p(y|x)-q(y|x)\|_{1}].

∎

Lemma A.2 (Error Propagation Dynamics).

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the environment transition operator mapping the joint distribution at time tt to the marginal history distribution at t+1t+1. Let Δt=‖dtπ−dtπ′‖1\Delta_{t}=\|d^{\pi}_{t}-d^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}\|_{1} and εt=𝔼h∼dtπ′∥π(⋅|h)−π′(⋅|h)∥1\varepsilon_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{h\sim d^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}}\|\pi(\cdot|h)-\pi^{\prime}(\cdot|h)\|_{1}. Assuming the start state distribution is fixed (Δ0=0\Delta_{0}=0), then for all t≥0t\geq 0:

Δt+1≤Δt+εt⟹Δt≤∑i=0t−1εi.\Delta_{t+1}\leq\Delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}\quad\implies\quad\Delta_{t}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}\varepsilon_{i}. (7)
Proof.

Let qtπ​(h,a)=dtπ​(h)​π​(a|h)q^{\pi}_{t}(h,a)=d^{\pi}_{t}(h)\pi(a|h) be the joint distribution at time tt. The transition to the next history ht+1h_{t+1} is deterministic given ht,ath_{t},a_{t} and the stochastic environment transition st+1∼P(⋅|st,at)s_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|s_{t},a_{t}). The operator mapping qt→dt+1q_{t}\to d_{t+1} is a linear map represented by a stochastic matrix, making it non-expansive in the ℓ1\ell_{1}-norm. Thus:

Δt+1=‖dt+1π−dt+1π′‖1≤‖qtπ−qtπ′‖1.\Delta_{t+1}=\|d^{\pi}_{t+1}-d^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t+1}\|_{1}\leq\|q^{\pi}_{t}-q^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}\|_{1}.

Applying Lemma A.1 to the RHS:

∥qtπ−qtπ′∥1≤∥dtπ−dtπ′∥1+𝔼h∼dtπ′∥π(⋅|h)−π′(⋅|h)∥1=Δt+εt.\|q^{\pi}_{t}-q^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}\|_{1}\leq\|d^{\pi}_{t}-d^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}\|_{1}+\mathbb{E}_{h\sim d^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}}\|\pi(\cdot|h)-\pi^{\prime}(\cdot|h)\|_{1}=\Delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}.

Combining these gives the recurrence Δt+1≤Δt+εt\Delta_{t+1}\leq\Delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}. Telescoping the sum from i=0i=0 to t−1t-1 with Δ0=0\Delta_{0}=0 yields the result. ∎

A.3 Proof of Theorem 3.1 (Performance Difference via Policy Shift)

Theorem 3.1. For any two policies π,π′\pi,\pi^{\prime} over finite horizon HH, the difference in expected return is bounded by:

|J⁡(π)−J⁡(π′)|≤Rmax​∑i=0H−1(H−i)​εi.|J(\pi)-J(\pi^{\prime})|\leq R_{\max}\sum_{i=0}^{H-1}(H-i)\varepsilon_{i}.
Proof.

The difference in expected return can be written as the sum of differences in expected rewards at each time step. Let qtπq^{\pi}_{t} denote the joint distribution of (h,a)(h,a) at time tt under policy π\pi.

|J⁡(π)−J⁡(π′)|\displaystyle|J(\pi)-J(\pi^{\prime})| =|∑t=0H−1(𝔼(h,a)∼qtπ​[r⁡(h,a)]−𝔼(h,a)∼qtπ′​[r⁡(h,a)])|\displaystyle=\left|\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\left(\mathbb{E}_{(h,a)\sim q^{\pi}_{t}}[r(h,a)]-\mathbb{E}_{(h,a)\sim q^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}}[r(h,a)]\right)\right|
≤∑t=0H−1|∑h,a(qtπ​(h,a)−qtπ′​(h,a))​r​(h,a)|.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\left|\sum_{h,a}(q^{\pi}_{t}(h,a)-q^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}(h,a))r(h,a)\right|.

Using Hölder’s inequality (bounding the expectation difference by the ℓ1\ell_{1} distance and max reward):

|∑h,a(qtπ​(h,a)−qtπ′​(h,a))​r​(h,a)|≤Rmax​‖qtπ−qtπ′‖1.\left|\sum_{h,a}(q^{\pi}_{t}(h,a)-q^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}(h,a))r(h,a)\right|\leq R_{\max}\|q^{\pi}_{t}-q^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}\|_{1}.

From the proof of Lemma A.2, we know ‖qtπ−qtπ′‖1≤Δt+εt\|q^{\pi}_{t}-q^{\pi^{\prime}}_{t}\|_{1}\leq\Delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}. Thus:

|J⁡(π)−J⁡(π′)|≤Rmax​∑t=0H−1(Δt+εt).|J(\pi)-J(\pi^{\prime})|\leq R_{\max}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}(\Delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}).

Substituting Δt≤∑j=0t−1εj\Delta_{t}\leq\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\varepsilon_{j}:

∑t=0H−1(Δt+εt)=∑t=0H−1(∑j=0t−1εj+εt)=∑t=0H−1∑j=0tεj.\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}(\Delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{t})=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\varepsilon_{j}+\varepsilon_{t}\right)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\sum_{j=0}^{t}\varepsilon_{j}.

By changing the order of summation, the term εi\varepsilon_{i} appears for every t≥it\geq i:

∑t=0H−1∑j=0tεj=∑i=0H−1(H−i)​εi.\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\sum_{j=0}^{t}\varepsilon_{j}=\sum_{i=0}^{H-1}(H-i)\varepsilon_{i}.

Multiplying by RmaxR_{\max} concludes the proof. ∎

A.4 Proof of Theorem 3.2 (Sim-to-Real Gap)

Theorem 3.2. For any fixed policy π\pi, let δt=𝔼(h,a)∼qtreal∥𝒯real(⋅|h,a)−𝒯sim(⋅|h,a)∥1\delta_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{(h,a)\sim q^{\text{real}}_{t}}\|\mathcal{T}_{\text{real}}(\cdot|h,a)-\mathcal{T}_{\text{sim}}(\cdot|h,a)\|_{1}. Then:

|Jreal​(π)−Jsim​(π)|≤Rmax​∑i=0H−1(H−i)​δi.|J_{\text{real}}(\pi)-J_{\text{sim}}(\pi)|\leq R_{\max}\sum_{i=0}^{H-1}(H-i)\delta_{i}.
Proof.

Let dtreald^{\text{real}}_{t} and dtsimd^{\text{sim}}_{t} denote the history distributions induced by π\pi in the real and simulated environments, respectively. Let Δtenv=‖dtreal−dtsim‖1\Delta^{\text{env}}_{t}=\|d^{\text{real}}_{t}-d^{\text{sim}}_{t}\|_{1}.

Since the policy π\pi is fixed in both environments, the joint distributions satisfy qtreal​(h,a)=dtreal​(h)​π​(a|h)q^{\text{real}}_{t}(h,a)=d^{\text{real}}_{t}(h)\pi(a|h) and qtsim​(h,a)=dtsim​(h)​π​(a|h)q^{\text{sim}}_{t}(h,a)=d^{\text{sim}}_{t}(h)\pi(a|h), so ‖qtreal−qtsim‖1=Δtenv\|q^{\text{real}}_{t}-q^{\text{sim}}_{t}\|_{1}=\Delta^{\text{env}}_{t}.

The value difference is bounded by the cumulative divergence in joint distributions plus the local transition errors:

|Jreal​(π)−Jsim​(π)|≤Rmax​∑t=0H−1(Δtenv+δt).|J_{\text{real}}(\pi)-J_{\text{sim}}(\pi)|\leq R_{\max}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}(\Delta^{\text{env}}_{t}+\delta_{t}).

This follows because at each step tt, the reward difference depends on the state at t+1t+1, which is influenced by both the history mismatch Δtenv\Delta^{\text{env}}_{t} and the current transition error δt\delta_{t}.

We now analyze the recurrence of Δtenv\Delta^{\text{env}}_{t}. The history distribution at t+1t+1 is obtained by applying the respective transition operators.

Δt+1env\displaystyle\Delta^{\text{env}}_{t+1} =‖𝒯real​(qtreal)−𝒯sim​(qtsim)‖1\displaystyle=\|\mathcal{T}_{\text{real}}(q^{\text{real}}_{t})-\mathcal{T}_{\text{sim}}(q^{\text{sim}}_{t})\|_{1}

Term (A) - Local Simulator Error: This measures the error of the simulator on the real distribution.

(A)\displaystyle(A) =∑h′,h,a|Preal​(h′|h,a)​qtreal​(h,a)−Psim​(h′|h,a)​qtreal​(h,a)|\displaystyle=\sum_{h^{\prime},h,a}|P_{\text{real}}(h^{\prime}|h,a)q^{\text{real}}_{t}(h,a)-P_{\text{sim}}(h^{\prime}|h,a)q^{\text{real}}_{t}(h,a)|

=𝔼(h,a)∼qtreal[∥𝒯real(⋅|h,a)−𝒯sim(⋅|h,a)∥1]=δt.\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{(h,a)\sim q^{\text{real}}_{t}}[\|\mathcal{T}_{\text{real}}(\cdot|h,a)-\mathcal{T}_{\text{sim}}(\cdot|h,a)\|_{1}]=\delta_{t}.

Thus, we have the recurrence Δt+1env≤Δtenv+δt\Delta^{\text{env}}_{t+1}\leq\Delta^{\text{env}}_{t}+\delta_{t}. Assuming Δ0env=0\Delta^{\text{env}}_{0}=0, this unfolds to Δtenv≤∑i=0t−1δi\Delta^{\text{env}}_{t}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}\delta_{i}. Substituting this back:

Appendix B Experimental Details

In this section, we provide a comprehensive description of the datasets, model configurations, training hyperparameters, and computational infrastructure used in our experiments. Our implementation builds on the SLIME distributed RL framework and the CollabLLM evaluation pipeline.

B.1 Datasets and Benchmarks

We evaluate our proposed framework on two distinct multi-turn dialogue domains that require long-horizon planning and precise information seeking.

MATH-Chat.

This benchmark evaluates the reasoning and tutoring capability of the agent in a conversational math problem-solving scenario.

  • •

    Data Source: We adapt problems from the MATH dataset Hendrycks et al. [2021], specifically selecting Hard-level problems that require multi-step reasoning.

  • •

    Task Setup: For each math problem, the ground-truth solution serves as y∗y^{*}. The user simulator plays the role of a student who may express confusion, make logical errors, or ask for clarification, requiring the agent to guide them step-by-step rather than directly revealing the answer.

  • •

    Statistics: The RL training set comprises ∼{\sim}3,000 problems (stored in Parquet format). Evaluation is conducted on a held-out set of 200 problems, with results averaged over 3 independent runs.

  • •

    Reward: Binary accuracy—an LLM judge (Qwen3-235B) determines whether the agent’s final answer matches the ground truth (R∈{0,1}R\in\{0,1\}).

MediumDocEdit-Chat.

This dataset focuses on collaborative document editing, requiring the agent to iteratively refine a document based on user feedback.

  • •

    Data Source: Derived from article writing and editing corpora. Each sample consists of an initial user request xx and a ground-truth refined document y∗y^{*}.

  • •

    Task Setup: The user provides ambiguous or incomplete editing instructions, requiring the agent to proactively ask clarifying questions and propose partial edits across multiple turns.

  • •

    Statistics: The RL training set contains ∼{\sim}38,118 editing prompts (Parquet format). Evaluation uses a held-out set of 200 samples, averaged over 3 runs.

  • •

    Reward: Sentence-level BLEU score between the agent’s final produced document and the ground-truth reference y∗y^{*} (R∈[0,1]R\in[0,1]).

B.2 Model Architectures

Policy Agent (πθ\pi_{\theta}).

We use Gemma-3-4B-IT Gemma Team et al. [2024] as the backbone for the dialogue policy across all experiments. This model is chosen for its strong instruction-following capabilities at a compact 4B parameter scale, which enables efficient on-policy rollout generation during interactive RL training. The model is loaded in bfloat16 precision with Flash Attention 2 enabled.

User Simulator (πϕsim\pi_{\phi}^{\text{sim}}).

We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct Qwen Team [2024] as the simulator backbone. The larger 7B scale (relative to the 4B policy) ensures the simulator has sufficient capacity to model diverse and realistic user behaviors. After Phase I SFT calibration, the simulator is frozen for Phase II training.

Evaluation Simulator & Judge.

During evaluation, we employ Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct (FP8 quantized) as both the user simulator and the accuracy/quality judge. This ensures evaluation is independent of the training-time simulator, providing an unbiased assessment of the policy’s generalization.

B.3 Training Phase I: Simulator Calibration (SFT)

In the first phase, we calibrate the user simulator via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on multi-turn interaction traces collected from the Qwen3-235B oracle simulator interacting with the base policy model. This is a behavioral cloning approach—the simulator learns to replicate realistic human-like interaction patterns.

Data Collection.

We deploy the Qwen3-235B model as an oracle user simulator (conditioned on ground-truth goals) and collect multi-turn trajectories by having it interact with the Gemma-3-4B-IT base model. This produces:

  • •

    MATH-Chat: 1,860 multi-turn trajectories (max sequence length: 4,096 tokens).

  • •

    MediumDocEdit-Chat: 16,028 multi-turn trajectories (max sequence length: 6,144 tokens).

Training Setup.

We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct using standard causal language modeling loss on the user turns only (masking assistant turns). Training uses FSDP on 8×8\times NVIDIA A800-80GB GPUs. Hyperparameters are detailed in Appendix D, Table 3.

B.4 Training Phase II: Interactive Policy Optimization (GRPO)

In the second phase, the SFT-calibrated simulator is frozen, and we optimize the policy agent πθ\pi_{\theta} via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) Shao et al. [2024]. GRPO eliminates the need for a separate value network by normalizing rewards within a group of sampled trajectories, making it memory-efficient for long-context multi-turn training.

Interaction Protocol.

For each training prompt xx, the agent generates G=32G=32 independent multi-turn trajectories by interacting with the aligned simulator. Each episode runs for up to H=7H=7 dialogue rounds (14 total turns). The simulator generates the first user message and the episode terminates upon the simulator emitting a [[TERMINATE CHAT]] signal or reaching the maximum turn count.

Reward Function.

We use sparse outcome rewards R⁡(τ)R(\tau) administered only at episode completion:

  • •

    MATH-Chat: Binary accuracy (0/1) determined by an LLM judge comparing the final answer to ground truth.

  • •

    MediumDocEdit-Chat: BLEU score between the final document and the reference.

Training Setup.

We train with Ray-based distributed FSDP on 32 GPUs (4 nodes ×\times 8 A800-80GB) with SGLang for efficient rollout generation. The policy and rollout engine are co-located on the same GPUs (--colocate mode). Full hyperparameters are in Appendix D, Table 4.

B.5 Baselines Implementation

Gemma-3-4B-IT (Base Model).

The original instruction-tuned model without any multi-turn RL fine-tuning, serving as the zero-shot baseline. We evaluate it with the same proactive system prompt used during RL training.

CollabLLM (Static RL).

We reproduce CollabLLM Wu et al. [2025] using the official codebase. CollabLLM represents the state-of-the-art in Static Context RL: it trains the policy on fixed offline conversation logs using Multi-turn-aware Rewards (MR). To ensure a fair comparison, we adapt CollabLLM to use Gemma-3-4B-IT as the backbone (matching our method), rather than the models used in their original paper. The reward model and training procedure follow their official implementation.

Ours (Static Context).

An ablation of our framework where the policy is trained via GRPO on static offline trajectories without dynamic simulator interaction. The policy optimizes against fixed conversation logs collected from the oracle simulator, conditioning on offline history h∼dtdatah\sim d^{\text{data}}_{t} rather than self-generated trajectories. This isolates the effect of closing the interaction loop.

Ours (Naive Interactive).

An ablation using the full interactive RL loop but with an uncalibrated user simulator. Specifically, we use the base Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model (without Phase I SFT) prompted to act as a user. This isolates the impact of simulator calibration from the benefit of interactive training.

B.6 Computational Infrastructure

  • •

    Hardware: All experiments were conducted on NVIDIA A800-80GB GPUs. Phase I uses 8 GPUs; Phase II uses 32 GPUs (4 nodes).

  • •

    Software: Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.x, SLIME (distributed RL framework), SGLang (efficient LLM serving for rollout generation), and the CollabLLM evaluation pipeline.

  • •

    Compute Cost: Phase I (SFT) completes in <<1 hour per task. Phase II (GRPO) trains for 10 steps (MATH) / 20 steps (MediumDocEdit), taking approximately 4–8 hours per task on 32 GPUs.

  • •

    Networking: NCCL communication with InfiniBand disabled (NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1); extended timeouts (72,000s) for long rollout steps.

Appendix C Prompts

This section presents the exact prompts used in our framework. We include: (1) the User Simulator prompt used during both Phase I calibration and Phase II interactive rollouts, (2) the Policy Agent (proactive assistant) instruction used during RL training, and (3) the Accuracy Judge prompt used for reward computation. Template variables populated at runtime are highlighted in {{blue}}.

C.1 User Simulator Prompt

The user simulator is conditioned on a task description and the ground-truth goal (reference answer), but is instructed to behave as a realistic human user—releasing information progressively, making occasional mistakes, and minimizing effort. This prompt is used both for the Qwen3-235B oracle (whose outputs serve as SFT targets in Phase I) and for the SFT-trained Qwen2.5-7B simulator during Phase II rollouts.

C.2 Policy Agent Prompt (Proactive Assistant)

The policy model receives this system-level instruction that encourages interactive, collaborative behavior. This prompt is used during both RL training and evaluation to guide the agent toward asking clarifying questions and providing structured assistance.

C.3 Accuracy Judge Prompt (Reward Function)

During Phase II training, we use an LLM-based accuracy judge as the reward function for MATH-Chat. The judge evaluates whether the policy’s final answer matches the ground truth. This prompt is sent to Qwen3-235B-Instruct.

Appendix D Implementation Details

This appendix provides full implementation details for reproducibility. Our framework consists of two training phases: Phase I (Simulator Calibration via SFT) and Phase II (Interactive Policy Optimization via GRPO).

D.1 Phase I: Simulator Calibration (SFT)

Base Model.

We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the backbone for the user simulator. This model is chosen for its strong instruction-following capabilities and multilingual performance, providing a robust foundation for behavioral cloning.

Datasets.

We collect multi-turn interaction traces from a high-fidelity oracle simulator (Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct) interacting with the base policy model. These traces capture realistic user behaviors including clarification requests, partial understanding expressions, and persistent goal pursuit. The resulting training sets are:

  • •

    MATH-Chat Simulator: 1,860 multi-turn trajectories, each containing the problem statement, ground-truth solution, and the oracle user’s turns. Maximum sequence length: 4,096 tokens.

  • •

    MediumDocEdit-Chat Simulator: 16,028 multi-turn trajectories capturing collaborative editing interactions. Maximum sequence length: 6,144 tokens.

Training Configuration.

We train with FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallelism) on 8×\times A800-80GB GPUs. The detailed hyperparameters are listed in Table 3.

D.2 Phase II: Interactive Policy Optimization (GRPO)

Base Model.

We use Gemma-3-4B-IT as the policy model backbone. This compact yet capable model enables efficient on-policy rollout generation during interactive RL training.

Datasets.

The RL training prompts consist of:

  • •

    MATH-Chat: ∼{\sim}3,000 math problems (from MATH-Hard) formatted as initial user queries in Parquet format.

  • •

    MediumDocEdit-Chat: ∼{\sim}38,118 article writing/editing prompts in Parquet format.

RL Algorithm.

We use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with the following key design choices:

  • •

    Advantage Estimation: Group-level normalization: A^​(τ)=(R⁡(τ)−μG)/σG\hat{A}(\tau)=(R(\tau)-\mu_{G})/\sigma_{G}, where GG is the group of trajectories sampled for the same prompt.

  • •

    Clipping: Asymmetric clipping with ϵlow=0.2\epsilon_{\text{low}}=0.2 and ϵhigh=0.28\epsilon_{\text{high}}=0.28.

  • •

    KL Regularization: Low-variance KL loss with coefficient β=0.0\beta=0.0 (effectively disabled, relying on clipping for stability).

  • •

    Reward: Binary accuracy oracle for MATH-Chat; BLEU score for MediumDocEdit-Chat.

Training Configuration.

We train with Ray-based distributed FSDP on 32 GPUs (4 nodes ×\times 8 GPUs) with SGLang for efficient rollout generation. The detailed hyperparameters are listed in Table 4.

Evaluation Setup.

All evaluations use Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct as both the user simulator and the evaluation judge during testing. This ensures that the evaluation is independent of the training-time simulator. Key evaluation parameters:

  • •

    Evaluation set size: 200 problems per domain

  • •

    Maximum dialogue turns: 14 (7 rounds of user-assistant exchange)

  • •

    Policy generation temperature: 0.8

  • •

    Results averaged over 3 independent runs

Appendix E Limitations and Future Work

While our work establishes a theoretical framework for mitigating distribution shift in interactive dialogue and demonstrates strong empirical results, we acknowledge certain limitations that point towards future research directions.

Computational Overhead. A primary limitation of the Calibrated Interactive RL framework is its computational demand during the training phase. Unlike Static Context RL, which only requires a single forward-backward pass over fixed offline datasets, our closed-loop paradigm necessitates running generation steps for both the policy agent and the user simulator during the rollout phase. This substantially increases the inference overhead and memory footprint, especially for long-horizon conversations. Future work could address this bottleneck by distilling the aligned simulator into a much smaller parameter-efficient model, or by exploring offline-to-online RL paradigms where the agent is pre-trained heavily on static logs and only fine-tuned interactively for a few critical turns to rectify specific distribution shifts.

Advanced Simulator Calibration. A second limitation lies in our current reliance on Supervised Fine-Tuning for Phase I simulator calibration. While behavioral cloning is highly effective for matching human distributions within the support of the training data, it may struggle to handle heavily out-of-distribution dialogue states dynamically induced by a rapidly exploring policy agent. In future work, we plan to extend simulator training beyond SFT by formulating it as a Reinforcement Learning problem. By optimizing the simulator to maximize a discriminator-derived "Realism Reward," it can proactively learn to maintain human-like stubbornness and constraints even in unobserved scenarios. Furthermore, drawing inspiration from Generative Adversarial Networks and adversarial imitation learning, a highly promising direction is to introduce an adversarial co-evolution framework. Instead of relying on a fixed, rule-based or static reward model, we could dynamically co-train a discriminator to distinguish between real human interaction logs and simulated trajectories. The simulator would be trained to actively fool this continuously evolving discriminator, establishing an auto-curriculum that mutually pushes both the dialogue policy and the simulator toward a higher level of behavioral fidelity and robustness.

Appendix F Case Study: Qualitative Analysis of MATH-Chat

To provide deeper insight into the behavioral differences between the base model and our Calibrated Interactive RL agent, we present representative case studies from the MATH-Chat evaluation. These examples illustrate how the trained policy achieves superior accuracy through improved reasoning efficiency, error avoidance, and effective multi-turn interaction.

F.1 Overview of Improvements

Out of 200 evaluation problems, we identify 29 cases where the baseline Gemma-3-4B-IT model fails (accuracy = 0) but our trained model succeeds (accuracy = 1). Table 5 summarizes representative cases across different mathematical domains.

F.2 Case Study 1: Nested Square Root Domain

This case demonstrates how the trained model avoids the “correction loop” failure mode that plagues the baseline. The problem requires finding the domain of f⁡(x)=x2−16−3f(x)=\sqrt{\sqrt{x^{2}-16}-3}.

Analysis. The baseline model exhibits a characteristic failure pattern: it misreads the function structure (combining −16-16 and −3-3 into a single expression x2−19x^{2}-19), and despite repeated user corrections over 14 turns, it never recovers from this structural misunderstanding. In contrast, our trained model correctly decomposes the problem into two independent constraints from the first response, demonstrating that interactive RL training enables the policy to develop more systematic problem-solving strategies.

F.3 Case Study 2: Direct Computation vs. Error Cascade

This case highlights how the trained model achieves efficiency through confident, correct computation, while the baseline gets trapped in unnecessary philosophical debates about function definitions.

Analysis. The trained model demonstrates two key improvements learned through interactive RL: (1) computational confidence—it directly evaluates each case without hedging, and (2) efficiency—it solves the problem in a single turn, avoiding unnecessary back-and-forth. The baseline’s failure stems from an overly cautious (and incorrect) claim about function domains, which it cannot self-correct even when the user provides explicit counterarguments.

F.4 Case Study 3: Correct Enumeration in Probability

This case demonstrates improved systematic reasoning in combinatorics.

Analysis. The baseline model suffers from an enumeration error cascade—once it incorrectly classifies some pairs as favorable, subsequent corrections only introduce new errors. Our trained model avoids this by: (1) first establishing an algebraic criterion (1−x)​(1−y)>−1(1-x)(1-y)>-1 that simplifies checking, and (2) systematically verifying each case. This algebraic-first approach is a reasoning strategy that emerges from RL training, where the model learns that systematic methods are more robust than ad-hoc enumeration.

F.5 Summary of Behavioral Patterns

Across the 29 improved cases, we identify three dominant patterns that distinguish our trained model from the baseline:

  1. 1.

    Direct Problem Solving (62% of cases): The trained model provides correct solutions in significantly fewer turns, avoiding the “try-and-fail” loops that characterize the baseline. Average turn reduction: 14 →\rightarrow 7 turns.

  2. 2.

    Structural Understanding (24% of cases): The trained model correctly parses complex mathematical expressions (nested functions, piecewise definitions) on the first attempt, while the baseline frequently misreads problem structure and cannot self-correct.

  3. 3.

    Algebraic Strategy (14% of cases): The trained model employs general algebraic manipulations before attempting numerical computation, reducing the chance of arithmetic errors that cascade through subsequent reasoning steps.

These patterns confirm that interactive RL training does not merely improve accuracy through memorization, but fundamentally changes the model’s problem-solving strategy—shifting from reactive error correction to proactive systematic reasoning.

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: As shown in Table 2, we report standard deviations for all main metrics. As stated in Appendix D (Line 691), these results are averaged over 3 independent evaluation runs to account for generation variance.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: Hardware specifics (8x to 32x NVIDIA A100/H100 80GB GPUs) and software frameworks (PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang) are detailed in Appendix B.6, along with placeholders for total compute hours.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: This research focuses on mathematical reasoning and collaborative document editing, utilizing standard datasets and adhering strictly to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [No]

  49. Justification: Given page limits, we focused heavily on theoretical proofs and methodology. While our framework significantly improves interactive AI capabilities, we acknowledge that highly proactive conversational agents could theoretically be misused for persuasive deception, which underscores the need for future safety alignment research.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The datasets (math problems, document edits) and the foundational models used (Llama-3, Qwen) are publicly available and do not pose a uniquely high risk for dual-use or misuse requiring specific safeguards.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: We properly cite the foundational models (Gemma3, Qwen2.5) and source datasets (e.g., MATH). We comply with their respective open-weight licenses and acceptable use policies.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: The data construction pipelines, statistics, and example domains for the newly derived multi-turn interaction datasets (MATH-Chat and MediumDocEdit-Chat) are detailed in Appendix B.1 and Appendix E.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  69. Justification: This work exclusively uses LLM-based user simulators and LLM-as-a-Judge for evaluation, and does not involve any human subjects or crowdsourcing.

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

  74. Justification: The research does not involve human subjects, hence IRB approval is not applicable.

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

    Declaration of LLM usage

Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required.
